bio: Dr. Marcus Åberg researches nutrition and body clocks in Stockholm. He has worked with shift workers, athletes and his own family, who still sometimes eat dinner too late.
bullets: How your body clock handles food
A gentle twelve-hour eating window, step by step
Meal timing for shift workers and parents

title: The Sitting Cure
author: Dr. Felix Oyelowo
tagline: Why your chair is the problem, and twelve moves that fix it
hook: Your chair is not your friend.
blurb:
Most of us sit for nine hours a day. Our bodies were built to move.
Dr. Felix Oyelowo, a sports medicine doctor, explains what long sitting does to your back, heart and blood sugar, and offers twelve simple moves you can do at your desk, at home or on the way to work. No gym, no special kit, just a better way to spend your day.
bio: Dr. Felix Oyelowo is a sports medicine doctor in Lagos and Manchester. He works with office workers and athletes, and he wrote this book standing up.
bullets: What long sitting does to your body
Twelve simple moves for desk and home
How to build movement into your workday

title: The Upright Year
author: Dr. Omar Haddaway
tagline: Twelve months to a strong, pain-free back
hook: A strong back is built a little at a time.
blurb:
Back pain is one of the most common reasons people miss work. Most of it gets better with movement, not rest.
Dr. Omar Haddaway, a spine specialist, offers a year-long plan: one simple habit each month, from how you sit to how you lift to how you sleep. Easy to follow, kind to beginners, and designed to keep your back strong for life.
bio: Dr. Omar Haddaway is a spine specialist and physiotherapist in Dubai. He has treated thousands of patients with back pain and stands at his desk, most of the time.
bullets: Twelve monthly habits for a stronger back
Gentle exercises for pain and stiffness
When to see a doctor, and what to ask

title: Thirty Plants a Week
author: Dr. Ana Lucía Paredes
tagline: The gut-health habit that feeds you more, not less
hook: Eat more, not less. Thirty different plants a week.
blurb:
Diet books usually ask you to cut things out. This one asks you to add things in.
Dr. Ana Lucía Paredes explains why eating a wide variety of plants, from beans and grains to herbs, nuts and spices, is one of the best things you can do for your gut. With easy tracking, shopping lists and fifty simple recipes, reaching thirty plants a week becomes easy, cheap and delicious.
bio: Dr. Ana Lucía Paredes is a gut-health researcher and dietitian in Bogotá and London. She grew up in a family of market traders and still counts her plants every week.
bullets: Why plant variety matters for your gut
A weekly tracker and shopping lists
Fifty simple recipes that add plants

title: Twenty-Two Feet of You
author: Dr. Priya Nandakumar
tagline: The new science of the gut, and how it runs the rest of you
hook: There are twenty-two feet of you that you never think about.
blurb:
Your gut is about seven metres long, home to trillions of microbes, and in constant conversation with your brain, your immune system and your mood.
Dr. Priya Nandakumar, a gastroenterologist, explains the new science of the gut in plain language and turns it into a simple plan: what to eat more of, what to stop worrying about, and the everyday habits that help your gut look after the rest of you.
bio: Dr. Priya Nandakumar is a consultant gastroenterologist in Birmingham. She has treated gut conditions for twenty years and is known for explaining hard science with a lot of patience.
bullets: How your gut talks to your brain and mood
A four-week plan to feed your gut well
What to ask your doctor, and when

title: A Ball in No Man's Land
author: Thomas Ellerby
hook: On Christmas Day 1914, enemies climbed out of the trenches and shook hands.
blurb:
Only months into the First World War, along stretches of the Western Front, soldiers on both sides stopped fighting. They sang carols, swapped gifts, buried their dead and, in some places, kicked a ball about.
Thomas Ellerby draws on letters and diaries from British and German soldiers to tell the true story of the Christmas truce: what happened, where, and why it was never allowed to happen again.
bio: Thomas Ellerby is a military historian who has spent twenty years reading soldiers' letters from the First World War. He lives in Ypres, close to where the truce took place.
bullets: The truce told through soldiers' own letters
What happened along different parts of the front
Why the generals made sure it never happened again

title: Ash Before Noon
author: Lucia Varrone
hook: By lunchtime the sky was falling.
blurb:
In 79 CE, Mount Vesuvius erupted above the busy Roman town of Pompeii. Within a day the town was buried, and with it thousands of lives.
Lucia Varrone uses the latest archaeology and the letters of Pliny the Younger, who watched from across the bay, to reconstruct that final day hour by hour. A gripping, human history of one of the most famous disasters of the ancient world.
bio: Lucia Varrone is an archaeologist who has excavated at Pompeii and Herculaneum for fifteen years. She lives in Naples, within sight of Vesuvius. Her grandparents farmed on its slopes.
bullets: The last day of Pompeii, hour by hour
What new excavations reveal about the victims
Pliny the Younger's eyewitness account

title: Eighty-Seven Hours
author: Daniel Rourke
tagline: Apollo 13 and the room that brought them home
hook: Two hundred thousand miles from home, something exploded.
blurb:
In April 1970, an oxygen tank burst on Apollo 13, crippling the spacecraft on its way to the Moon. Three astronauts had limited air, power and water. The only way home was round the far side of the Moon.
Daniel Rourke tells the story of the eighty-seven hours that followed, and of the engineers in Mission Control who solved one impossible problem after another to bring the crew back alive.
bio: Daniel Rourke is a science writer and historian of spaceflight. He has interviewed dozens of former flight controllers and engineers and lives in Houston. He keeps a piece of mission-control carpet on his desk.
bullets: The explosion and the race to save the crew
The engineers and flight controllers behind the rescue
What Apollo 13 taught NASA about failure

title: Fireworks over Edo
author: Kentaro Walsh-Mori
hook: Before it was Tokyo, it was the largest city on Earth.
blurb:
For more than two centuries, Edo was the capital of the shoguns and home to over a million people. It was a city of bridges, theatres, bathhouses, fires and summer fireworks over the Sumida River.
Kentaro Walsh-Mori brings Edo to life through its streets, its people and the woodblock prints that recorded them, and shows how the old city still shapes modern Tokyo.
bio: Kentaro Walsh-Mori is a historian of Japan born in Kyoto and raised in Ireland. He teaches in Tokyo and leads walking tours of what remains of old Edo.
bullets: Daily life in the shoguns' capital
Fires, floods and the rebuilding of the city
Edo through the woodblock prints of its age

title: Seven Queens, One Throne
author: Eleanor Fairclough
tagline: The women who fought for England's crown
hook: One crown. Seven women who wanted it.
blurb:
England's history is often told through its kings. But again and again, women fought for the throne, ruled through others, or held the country together when the men failed.
Eleanor Fairclough tells the stories of seven queens and would-be queens, from the medieval Empress Matilda to Elizabeth I, and shows how each one changed what power could look like. A sweeping, readable history of crowns won and lost.
bio: Eleanor Fairclough is a historian of medieval and Tudor England. She has written widely on royal women and lives in Winchester, once England's capital. She is a regular voice on history radio.
bullets: Seven women who fought for England's crown
How each queen won, lost or held power
The myths and the evidence behind their stories

title: The Night Parliament Burned
author: Caroline Ashworth-Deane
hook: London watched as the heart of the nation went up in flames.
blurb:
On the evening of 16 October 1834, a fire started in the old Palace of Westminster. By morning most of the ancient building was gone. Crowds lined the Thames to watch, and among them was the painter J. M. W. Turner.
Caroline Ashworth-Deane tells the story of that night, how the fire began, who fought it, and how the disaster gave Britain the Parliament building we know today.
bio: Caroline Ashworth-Deane is a historian of nineteenth-century London. She has written about the city's fires, floods and rebuildings and lives within sight of the Thames.
bullets: How a careless job started a great fire
The night told by those who watched it
How the ruins became today's Parliament

title: The Queen Without a Tomb
author: Khalida Mansour
hook: She was one of the most powerful women in ancient Egypt. Then she disappeared.
blurb:
Nefertiti ruled beside the pharaoh Akhenaten during one of the strangest periods in Egyptian history. Her famous face is known around the world, but her tomb has never been found.
Khalida Mansour, an Egyptologist, follows the clues: the inscriptions, the art, the mummies and the theories, and asks what really happened to the queen. A gripping detective story that spans three thousand years, from the royal city of Amarna to the laboratories of today.
bio: Khalida Mansour is an Egyptologist who has worked on excavations at Amarna and in the Valley of the Kings. She teaches in Cairo and Oxford.
bullets: Nefertiti's life and power at Akhenaten's side
The search for her missing tomb
What the latest research suggests

title: The Silk Thread
author: Mei-Lin Hargreaves
tagline: How one road wove the world together, 200 BCE to 1450
hook: A thread of silk tied the ancient world together.
blurb:
For nearly two thousand years, caravans carried silk, spices, paper and ideas between China and the Mediterranean. Along the way, religions spread, cities rose, and empires met.
Mei-Lin Hargreaves follows the thread of the Silk Road from its beginnings to the age of sea routes, through the merchants, monks and travellers who made it, and shows how one trade connected the world.
bio: Mei-Lin Hargreaves is a historian of Central Asia. She has travelled the old Silk Road routes from Xi'an to Samarkand and teaches world history in Edinburgh.
bullets: How the Silk Road grew from a trade in cloth
The people, faiths and ideas that travelled it
Why the old routes faded, and what replaced them

title: The Summer That Never Came
author: Hannah Rossiter
tagline: 1816, a volcano, and a world without a harvest
hook: In 1816, it snowed in July.
blurb:
In April 1815, the volcano Tambora erupted in Indonesia, one of the largest eruptions in history. The ash spread around the world, and the following year summer did not arrive. Crops failed from New England to Switzerland and China.
Hannah Rossiter tells the story of the year without a summer: the hunger, the migrations and the strange art and ideas it left behind.
bio: Hannah Rossiter is a climate historian who studies how past eruptions and weather changed societies. She lives in Vermont, where 1816 is still remembered as eighteen-hundred-and-froze-to-death.
bullets: How one eruption changed the world's weather
Hunger and migration across three continents
The art and ideas born in a cold, dark year

title: The Tulip Crash
author: Pieter van der Laan
hook: For a few months, a single flower bulb was worth more than a house.
blurb:
In the winter of 1636, the Dutch went mad for tulips. Rare bulbs changed hands in taverns for fortunes. Then, in February 1637, the buyers vanished, and the market collapsed overnight.
Pieter van der Laan tells the story through the growers, traders and families who rode the bubble, and asks how much of the legend is true. A vivid, surprising history of the first great financial mania.
bio: Pieter van der Laan is a Dutch economic historian who has spent fifteen years in the archives of Haarlem. He lives in Leiden and grows tulips, at a sensible price.
bullets: How a flower became a financial craze
The people who won and lost fortunes
What the tulip crash teaches about bubbles today

title: The Women Who Ran Amsterdam
author: Marieke de Graaf
tagline: Wives, widows and traders of the Dutch Golden Age
hook: Behind the merchants of Amsterdam stood their wives, widows and daughters.
blurb:
In the seventeenth century, Amsterdam was the richest city in the world. Visitors were shocked to find women running shops, signing contracts and managing family fortunes.
Marieke de Graaf uses letters, account books and portraits to tell the stories of these women, from brewers and printers to shipping widows, and shows how they shaped the Dutch Golden Age. Their names were nearly forgotten. This book gives them back.
bio: Marieke de Graaf is a social historian at a university in Amsterdam. She has spent years in the city archives reading the account books of its forgotten businesswomen.
bullets: The women who ran shops, ships and fortunes
Life in Amsterdam at the height of its wealth
What their letters and accounts reveal

title: The Wreck of the Morning Star
author: James Trevanion
tagline: A storm, a pier, and a town that would not let them drown
hook: When the ship struck the sands, the whole town ran to the sea.
blurb:
On a winter night off the Norfolk coast, a sailing ship ran aground in a storm. As the waves broke over her, the people of a small seaside town launched their boats, again and again, to bring the crew ashore.
James Trevanion tells a story of courage on the coast, built from the history of Britain's early lifeboat crews and the towns that sent them out.
bio: James Trevanion is a maritime historian from Cornwall. He has crewed with a volunteer lifeboat station for ten years and writes about the history of rescue at sea.
bullets: The early history of lifeboat rescue
How coastal towns faced the sea together
A night of courage, told hour by hour

title: Twelve Weeks at Bletchley
author: Helen Carrick
hook: They broke the code that could have lost the war.
blurb:
In 1940, a small team at Bletchley Park raced to read Germany's Enigma messages. Every day the settings changed. Every day the clock started again.
Helen Carrick follows twelve weeks in the life of the codebreakers, mathematicians, linguists and young women operators who worked in secret, and shows how their work changed the course of the Second World War. A tense, human story of puzzles, pressure and secrecy.
bio: Helen Carrick is a historian of intelligence and wartime Britain. Her grandmother worked at Bletchley Park and never spoke of it until she was ninety.
bullets: How the Enigma machine worked
The people of Bletchley Park, many of them women
How broken codes changed the war at sea

title: Twenty-Six Miles to Athens
author: Andreas Kalogerou
tagline: Marathon, 490 BCE, and the run that saved a city
hook: A small army, an impossible victory, and a run into legend.
blurb:
In 490 BCE, a Persian army landed at Marathon, twenty-six miles from Athens. The Athenians were outnumbered and alone. What happened next saved their city and gave the world a famous race.
Andreas Kalogerou brings the battle and the legend of the runner to life, separating myth from evidence and showing why a single day in ancient Greece still shapes our world.
bio: Andreas Kalogerou is a historian of ancient Greece at a university in Athens. He has run the Marathon to Athens route three times, slowly, he admits.
bullets: The Battle of Marathon, step by step
The truth behind the legend of the runner
Why Athens's survival mattered for the world

title: Blistered
author: Diego Santamaría
hook: Fire makes everything taste better.
blurb:
Diego Santamaría learned to cook over wood and charcoal in his family's restaurant in Oaxaca. Fire, he says, is an ingredient.
Blistered teaches how to build and control a fire, and how to use it for vegetables, meat, fish, bread and even dessert. With clear guidance for small barbecues, big grills and city balconies. Every recipe has a version for an ordinary kitchen grill, so you can cook with fire flavour all year round.
bio: Diego Santamaría is a chef from Oaxaca who now cooks in Los Angeles. He has cooked over open fire on four continents and never travels without matches.
bullets: How to build and control a cooking fire
Recipes for vegetables, meat, fish and bread
Salsas and sauces to finish every dish

title: Citrus Year
author: Marisol Estevez
tagline: Lemons, oranges and limes through twelve months
hook: Bring a little sunshine into every month.
blurb:
Citrus is at its best in the coldest months, just when we need it most. Marisol Estevez grew up among orange groves in Valencia and cooks with lemons, limes and oranges all year round.
Citrus Year moves month by month through bright cakes, marmalades, salads, curds and drinks, with tips on choosing, zesting and preserving every kind of citrus fruit.
bio: Marisol Estevez is a pastry chef from Valencia who now lives in Bristol. She keeps a lemon tree in a pot on her kitchen windowsill, against all advice.
bullets: Seventy citrus recipes, month by month
Marmalades, curds and preserved lemons
A guide to every kind of citrus fruit

title: Fold & Pinch
author: Lucy Zhao-Pemberton
tagline: Dumplings, buns and parcels from a home kitchen
hook: Every family has a dumpling. Here are fifty.
blurb:
Dumplings are made by hand, often by many hands around one table. Lucy Zhao-Pemberton learned to fold them with her grandmother in Shanghai.
Fold & Pinch teaches the doughs, fillings and folds for fifty dumplings, buns and parcels from China and beyond, with step-by-step drawings and freezer tips so you can always have a batch ready. There are vegetarian fillings for every chapter and dipping sauces to finish.
bio: Lucy Zhao-Pemberton was born in Shanghai and grew up in Leeds. She teaches dumpling-making classes and can fold eighteen pleats without looking. Her family make two thousand dumplings every New Year.
bullets: Doughs, fillings and folds, step by step
Fifty dumplings, buns and parcels
How to freeze and cook from frozen

title: Forkful
author: Giulia Benedetti
tagline: Pasta for every night of the week
hook: A different pasta for every night of the week, and then some.
blurb:
Giulia Benedetti grew up above her family's trattoria in Bologna, where pasta was dinner most nights and nobody ever got bored.
Forkful collects one hundred of her favourite dishes, from five-ingredient weeknight bowls to slow Sunday ragù, with clear guidance on choosing the right shape, cooking it perfectly and making fresh pasta by hand when you have the time. Every recipe serves two to six and most take under thirty minutes.
bio: Giulia Benedetti is a cook and teacher from Bologna who now lives in London. She runs pasta classes in her kitchen and has never once broken spaghetti in half.
bullets: One hundred pasta recipes, quick to slow
How to match the shape to the sauce
Fresh pasta by hand, step by step

title: Know Your Beans
author: Leila Sorensen
tagline: Chickpeas, lentils and beans, cooked a hundred good ways
hook: The cheapest, healthiest food in your kitchen is also the most delicious.
blurb:
Beans, lentils and chickpeas are cheap, filling and good for you, but most of us cook only two or three recipes with them.
Leila Sorensen offers one hundred dishes from around the world: stews, salads, soups, dips and bakes. She shows how to cook dried beans perfectly, how to make tins taste great and how to build a week of meals around a single pot.
bio: Leila Sorensen is a food writer and nutritionist who grew up between Copenhagen and Beirut. She cooks a pot of beans every Sunday and has done for twenty years.
bullets: One hundred bean, lentil and chickpea dishes
How to cook dried beans perfectly
A week of meals from one Sunday pot

title: Market Day Vegetables
author: Agnes Duval
tagline: One hundred dishes from the weekly stall
hook: Go to the market. Come home. Cook what you found.
blurb:
Agnes Duval shops the way her grandmother did: once a week at the market, buying what looks best and deciding dinner later.
Market Day Vegetables offers one hundred simple dishes organised by vegetable, from cabbage and leeks to beans and squash, so you can buy what is fresh and cheap and still know what to make. Most recipes are vegetarian; all are easy.
bio: Agnes Duval is a French cook and writer who lives in Lyon and shops at the same market every Saturday. She has cooked more cabbage than she can count.
bullets: One hundred recipes, sorted by vegetable
Seasonal shopping guides
Mostly vegetarian, all easy

title: Masala Box
author: Anjali Mehra-Shaw
tagline: Seven spices, seventy recipes, one steel tin
hook: Seven spices. Seventy recipes. One steel tin.
blurb:
In almost every Indian kitchen there is a round steel spice box, the masala dabba, holding the seven spices a cook reaches for every day.
Anjali Mehra-Shaw shows how to fill your own and use it to cook seventy home-style dishes from across India, from Punjabi dal to Kerala fish curry. Clear, warm and practical, it is the book she wished she had when she first left home.
bio: Anjali Mehra-Shaw grew up in Delhi and Chennai and now cooks and teaches in Manchester. She has carried her mother's masala dabba across three countries.
bullets: How to fill and use a masala dabba
Seventy home-style recipes from across India
Weeknight meals in thirty minutes or less

title: Morning Pour
author: Tomás Arango
tagline: Coffee at home, from beans to the last good cup
hook: Better coffee at home, starting tomorrow morning.
blurb:
Good coffee does not need an expensive machine. It needs fresh beans, the right grind and a little care.
Tomás Arango, a coffee roaster from Colombia, explains every home method, from French press to pour-over to stovetop espresso, and shows how to choose beans, dial in your brew and make café-style milk drinks at home. Clear, friendly and full of tips from twenty years behind the roaster.
bio: Tomás Arango grew up on a coffee farm in Colombia and now roasts coffee in Copenhagen. He drinks three cups a day and remembers where every bean came from.
bullets: Every home brewing method, step by step
How to choose and store beans
Café-style milk drinks without a big machine

title: Open Crumb
author: Sam Whitford
hook: Great sourdough is mostly patience. This book supplies the rest.
blurb:
The open crumb, those big glossy holes in a good loaf, is every home baker's goal. Getting there takes flour, water, salt and time, and a little know-how.
Sam Whitford, a baker for twenty years, explains sourdough from the starter up, with clear timetables that fit around a working week and fixes for every flat, dense or sour loaf along the way.
bio: Sam Whitford has baked bread professionally for twenty years and now teaches sourdough classes in Somerset. Their starter is older than their children. They bake every morning before sunrise.
bullets: A starter you can make in seven days
Weekday and weekend baking timetables
A troubleshooting guide for every problem loaf

title: Room for Cake
author: Bea Hollister
tagline: Sixty bakes for after dinner, every day of the week
hook: There is always room for cake.
blurb:
Bea Hollister believes cake belongs to every day, not just birthdays.
Room for Cake offers sixty bakes for after dinner: simple loaf cakes, tray bakes, cheesecakes, puddings and a few showstoppers. Most can be made in an hour with one bowl, and each comes with tips for making ahead, freezing and fixing mistakes. There are gluten-free and dairy-free versions of many recipes, so everyone at the table gets a slice.
bio: Bea Hollister is a baker and teacher from Brighton. She has run a cake stall at the same market for twelve years and still tastes every batch.
bullets: Sixty bakes, most in one bowl
Make-ahead and freezing tips
How to fix a sunk, dry or cracked cake

title: Small Pan Suppers
author: Kit Abernethy
tagline: Dinners for one or two, made in a single pan
hook: Dinner for one or two, made in a single pan.
blurb:
Cooking for one or two can feel like too much effort for too little reward. Kit Abernethy thinks it should be the opposite.
Small Pan Suppers offers seventy dinners made in one frying pan or saucepan, scaled for one or two, using what is already in the fridge. Quick to cook, quick to wash up, and generous on flavour. Every recipe also doubles easily for guests.
bio: Kit Abernethy is a food writer who has lived alone in small flats in Edinburgh, Berlin and Lisbon. They cook every night in the same well-worn pan.
bullets: Seventy one-pan dinners for one or two
Smart shopping with no waste
Most dishes ready in thirty minutes

title: Sumac & Smoke
author: Rami Khoury
tagline: Fire, spice and sharing plates from a Levantine kitchen
hook: Fire, spice and a table full of people.
blurb:
Rami Khoury grew up between Beirut and Amman, where food was cooked over charcoal and always shared.
Sumac & Smoke brings that kitchen home with grilled meats and vegetables, bright salads, dips, flatbreads and the spice blends that tie them together. Most dishes work on a barbecue or under a home grill, and many can be made ahead for a crowd.
bio: Rami Khoury is a chef who grew up in Beirut and Amman. He now runs a restaurant in Melbourne built around a charcoal grill and a very long table.
bullets: Grilled dishes for barbecue or home grill
Mezze, dips and flatbreads
How to make and use your own spice blends

title: The Plum Year
author: Elsie Marchbank
tagline: Cakes, jams and slow puddings from one tree
hook: One tree. Twelve months. More plums than you know what to do with.
blurb:
When Elsie Marchbank inherited her grandmother's old plum tree, she also inherited the problem: hundreds of plums arriving all at once.
The Plum Year follows that tree through the seasons, with cakes, crumbles, jams, chutneys and slow puddings to use every fruit, and ways to bottle and freeze the harvest for the colder months. Many recipes also work with apricots, damsons, cherries and the other stone fruits that arrive in late summer.
bio: Elsie Marchbank is a baker and food writer who lives in Worcestershire, in a house with a very productive plum tree and a cupboard full of jam.
bullets: Cakes, bakes and puddings with plums
Jams, chutneys and ways to preserve
How to look after a fruit tree

title: Tomato Season
author: Rosa Kettleby
tagline: From the first green ones to the last sweet glut
hook: Follow the tomato from its first green weeks to its last sweet glut.
blurb:
Tomatoes change all summer long. The early ones are sharp and firm, the late ones soft, sweet and too many to eat.
Rosa Kettleby, a market gardener, cooks through the whole season month by month: green tomato chutneys in June, salads in July, roasting trays in August and the big September sauce-making days. With growing notes for anyone with a pot or a plot.
bio: Rosa Kettleby runs a small market garden in Kent where she grows forty kinds of tomato. She cooks for the farm's summer suppers and still eats tomatoes like apples.
bullets: Eighty recipes, month by month
How to grow tomatoes in pots or plots
Preserving the glut: sauces, chutneys and passata

title: Big Year 2027
hook: Set big goals. Break them into weeks.
blurb: Big Year is a goal planner for 2027. Start with a full year of goals, break each one into monthly steps, then plan the week ahead with space to track progress and review what worked. Bold, simple and built to keep you moving all year.
bullets: Yearly, monthly and weekly goal pages
Quarterly reviews to keep you on track
Habit tracker and project pages

title: Deep Hours
tagline: A focus planner: 90 days, 3 blocks a day
hook: Three blocks of deep work a day, for ninety days.
